verses.translation: And I saw{H7200} one{H259} lamb{H7716} standing{H5975} upon Mount{H2022} Tsiyon{H6726}, and with him a hundred{H3967} and four{H702} and forty{H705} thousand{H505}; and upon them was written{H3789} the name{H8034} of his Father{H1}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses שֶׂה (seh, H7716) — the specific Passover lamb from Exodus 12:3-5 (שֶׂה לְבֵית אָבוֹת — 'a lamb per household'). Greek uses ἀρνίον, a generic diminutive 'little lamb.' A back-translator from Greek would more likely use כֶּבֶשׂ (keves) or טָלֶה (taleh). The consistent use of seh throughout this Hebrew text ties the messianic figure directly to the Passover.

Uses הַר צִיּוֹן (Har Tsiyon, H2022+H6726) — the specific mountain of YHWH's dwelling in the Psalms (Ps 2:6, 48:2, 125:1) and prophets (Isa 2:3, 4:5, 24:23, Joel 3:5). This is natural Hebrew usage; the Greek Σιών is a transliteration.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'the name of his Father' (only the Father's name). Greek: τὸ ὄνομα αὐτοῦ καὶ τὸ ὄνομα τοῦ πατρὸς αὐτοῦ — 'HIS name AND his Father's name.' Greek adds the Lamb's name. A back-translator from Greek would not omit the Lamb's name.
Hebrew: 'upon them' (עליהם) — unspecified location. Greek: 'on their foreheads' (ἐπὶ τῶν μετώπων αὐτῶν). The Hebrew is less specific.
translation_notes: Tsiyon is transliterated from the Hebrew צִיּוֹן rather than anglicized as 'Zion.'
textual_notes: Psalm 2:6 — 'I have set my king upon Tsiyon, my holy mountain.' The lamb standing on Har Tsiyon directly fulfills the messianic-king enthronement psalm.

verses.translation: And I heard{H8085} one{H259} voice{H6963} from the heavens{H8064}, like the roaring{H7494} of great{H1419} waters{H4325}, and like the sound{H6963} of great{H1419} thunders{H6963}; and the voice{H6963} that I heard{H8085} was like the sound{H6963} of a harp{H3658}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses רַעַשׁ (ra'ash, H7494 — 'earthquake/roaring/tumult') for the sound of waters. Greek has φωνήν ('voice/sound'). Ra'ash is used in Ezekiel 3:12-13 for the sound of YHWH's glory departing (קוֹל רַעַשׁ גָּדוֹל — 'a sound of great tumult'). A back-translator from Greek's generic 'sound' would not reach for the Ezekiel glory-departure verb.

Uses קוֹלוֹת (kolot, H6963 — 'thunders') — the specific word for the thunders at Sinai (Ex 19:16: וַיְהִי קֹלֹת וּבְרָקִים — 'and there were thunders and lightnings'). Greek uses βροντῆς ('thunder'). A back-translator would use רעם (ra'am — 'thunder'), not the Sinai-specific kolot.

Uses כִּינּוֹר (kinnor, H3658) — David's specific instrument (1 Sam 16:16,23; 2 Sam 6:5; Ps 33:2, 71:22, 150:3). Greek has κιθαρῳδῶν κιθαριζόντων ἐν ταῖς κιθάραις αὐτῶν ('harpers harping on their harps') — a triple expansion. The Hebrew uses a single word with deep Davidic associations.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'like the sound of a harp' (single concise phrase). Greek: 'like harpers harping on their harps' (triple expansion). The Hebrew is characteristically terse.
Greek adds 'from heaven' (ἐκ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ) and uses 'many waters' (ὑδάτων πολλῶν) where Hebrew has 'great waters' (מים גדולים).
translation_notes: 'Roaring' for ra'ash captures the seismic/overwhelming quality — this is not a gentle sound but an earthquake-like rumble.
'Thunders' for kolot: this word means both 'voices' and 'thunders' in Hebrew. Context and the Sinai echo demand 'thunders.'
textual_notes: Ezekiel 43:2 — 'And behold, the glory of the God of Israel came from the east. And his voice was like the sound of many waters (כְּקוֹל מַיִם רַבִּים).' The Hebrew Revelation draws on this Ezekiel theophany imagery.

verses.translation: And they sang{H2167} as a new{H2319} song{H7892} before{H6440} the throne{H3678} and before{H6440} the four{H702} living-creatures{H2416} and the elders{H2205}; and no one{H259} was able{H3201} to learn{H3925} that song{H7892} except those hundred{H3967} and four{H702} and forty{H705} thousand{H505} who were acquired{H7069} from the ground{H127}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses מְזַמְּרִים (mezammerim, H2167 — 'singing/making music') — the specific word for musical worship in the Psalms (Ps 27:6, 57:8, 66:2, 68:5, 105:2). Greek ᾄδουσιν is generic 'they sing.' The Hebrew word connotes instrumental worship, not mere singing.

Uses אֲדָמָה (adamah, H127 — 'ground/soil') NOT אֶרֶץ (erets — 'earth/land'). Greek uses γῆ (ge — 'earth'). Same distinction as Revelation 21:1 — adamah echoes Genesis 2:7 where man was formed from the adamah. A back-translator from Greek would use ארץ, not the Genesis-laden adamah.

Uses שֶׁקָּנָה (she-qanah — 'who acquired,' ACTIVE voice, 3ms perfect of קנה H7069). Greek uses ἠγοράσθησαν ('were purchased' — PASSIVE voice). The Hebrew says the Lamb/YHWH actively acquired them; the Greek says they were passively bought. A back-translator from Greek passive would write שֶׁנִּקְנוּ (she-niqnu — passive), not the active form.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'as a new song' (כשיר חדש — with comparative כ, 'like/as a song'). Greek: ᾠδὴν καινήν ('a new song' — with ὡς 'as if'). Both use the simile but the Hebrew prefix כ is more terse.
Hebrew: 'acquired from the ground' (active, from adamah). Greek: 'redeemed from the earth' (passive, from ge). Different voice, different word for earth.
translation_notes: 'Sang' for mezammerim — the root zamar encompasses both singing and instrumental music-making. The Psalms use this word for accompanied worship.
'Ground' for adamah (not 'earth') preserves the Genesis 2:7 theological connection — they were acquired from the very soil from which Adam was formed.
textual_notes: Psalm 40:3 — 'He put a new song (שִׁיר חָדָשׁ) in my mouth.' The Hebrew 'new song' is a recurrent OT motif (Ps 33:3, 96:1, 98:1, 144:9, 149:1, Isa 42:10).

verses.translation: And these are those who did not sin{H2398} with the women{H802} — [and they are] like virgins{H1330} — and they walk{H1980} after{H310} the lamb{H7716}; and they are acquired{H7069} as firstfruits{H1061} for YHWH{H3068} and the lamb{H7716}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses חָטְאוּ (chat'u — 'sinned', from חטא H2398). Greek says οὐκ ἐμολύνθησαν ('were not defiled'). The Hebrew frames it as SIN; the Greek frames it as ritual DEFILEMENT. A back-translator from Greek would use לֹא נִטְמְאוּ (lo nitme'u — 'were not defiled', from טמא H2930), not the sin-verb חטא.

CRITICAL: Uses כִּבְתוּלוֹת (ki-vtulot — 'LIKE virgins', H1330) with the comparative prefix כ ('like/as'). This is a SIMILE. Greek says παρθένοι γάρ εἰσιν ('for they ARE virgins') — a statement of identity. The Hebrew says they are LIKE virgins; the Greek says they ARE virgins. A back-translator from Greek would write בתולות הם ('they are virgins'), not the simile כבתולות.

Uses בִּכּוּרוֹת (bikkurot — 'firstfruits', H1061) — the specific Temple harvest-offering term (Ex 23:16,19; 34:22,26; Num 18:13; Deut 26:10). This is the Shavuot/Weeks offering. Greek ἀπαρχή also means 'firstfruit' but the Hebrew form specifically evokes the Temple festival offering.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'sinned with women' (moral transgression). Greek: 'not defiled with women' (ritual impurity). Different categories — sin vs. defilement.
Hebrew: 'LIKE virgins' (simile with כ). Greek: 'ARE virgins' (identity claim). Fundamentally different assertion.
Hebrew: 'firstfruits for YHWH and the lamb.' Greek: 'firstfruit to God and to the Lamb' (τῷ θεῷ). Hebrew uses the Tetragrammaton; Greek uses θεός.
translation_notes: The bracket [וְהֵם] in the source suggests editorial restoration of a damaged passage.
'Firstfruits' for bikkurot — the Shavuot/Pentecost offering of the first harvest yield, presented at the Temple. The 144,000 are the harvest offering to YHWH.
textual_notes: Leviticus 23:17 — 'You shall bring from your dwellings two loaves of bread for a wave offering... they are firstfruits (בִּכּוּרִים) to YHWH.' The 144,000 as bikkurot connects them to the Shavuot offering.

verses.translation: And there is no{H369} deceit{H7423} in their spirit{H7307}, and they are innocent{H5355} before{H6440} the throne{H3678} of YHWH{H3068}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses בְּרוּחָם (be-rucham — 'in their spirit', H7307). Greek says ἐν τῷ στόματι αὐτῶν ('in their MOUTH'). The Hebrew locates truthfulness in the inner spirit; the Greek locates it in outward speech. A back-translator from Greek would write בְּפִיהֶם (be-fihem — 'in their mouth'), not ברוחם ('in their spirit'). This is a massive difference — inner integrity vs. verbal accuracy.

Uses נְקִיִּים (neqiyyim — 'innocent/clean', H5355) — the specific word for those innocent of bloodguilt (Ex 23:7; Deut 19:10, 21:8-9; 2 Kings 21:16, 24:4). Greek says ἄμωμοι ('without blemish' — a sacrificial term). A back-translator from Greek would use תְּמִימִים (temimim — 'unblemished'), the standard sacrificial-quality word. The Hebrew author frames them as judicially innocent, not sacrificially perfect.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'in their spirit' (רוחם). Greek: 'in their mouth' (στόματι). Different seat of truthfulness — internal vs. external.
Hebrew: 'innocent' (נקיים — judicial acquittal). Greek: 'without blemish' (ἄμωμοι — sacrificial quality). Different conceptual frame.
translation_notes: רְמִיָּה (remiyyah, H7423 — 'deceit/treachery') — used in the Psalms for inner duplicity (Ps 32:2, 34:14, 52:4, 101:7, 120:2). The Hebrew specifically targets inward deceit, consistent with 'in their spirit.'
'Innocent' for neqiyyim captures the judicial/legal sense — declared not guilty, free of blood.
textual_notes: Psalm 32:2 — 'Blessed is the man to whom YHWH imputes no iniquity, and in whose spirit (רוח) there is no deceit (רמיה).' The Hebrew Revelation quotes this psalm nearly verbatim.

verses.translation: And I saw{H7200} one{H259} messenger{H4397} hovering{H7363} in the midst{H8432} of the heavens{H8064}, and he had one proclamation-tablet to make known{H3045} to those dwelling upon the earth{H776} and to all{H3605} the peoples{H5971} and nations{H3816}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses רֹחֵף (rochef, H7363 — 'hovering') — one of the rarest verbs in the entire OT, appearing only in Genesis 1:2 (the Spirit of God 'hovering' over the waters — מְרַחֶפֶת) and Deuteronomy 32:11 (an eagle 'hovering' over its young). Greek uses πετόμενον ('flying'). A back-translator from Greek 'flying' would use עָף (uf — 'fly', H5774), the common word. NO translator would independently reach for the ultra-rare Genesis creation verb. The messenger hovers like the Spirit at creation.

CRITICAL: Uses אֵוַן גֵּילִיוֹן as the object the messenger carries. Greek has εὐαγγέλιον αἰώνιον ('eternal gospel'). The Hebrew compound phonetically resembles 'euangelion' but parses as two Hebrew words: אֵוַן (possibly a variant of אֶבֶן — 'stone') and גֵּילִיוֹן (from גלה H1540 — 'to reveal'; cf. Isaiah 8:1 where גִּלָּיוֹן means 'tablet'). The Hebrew author either (a) hears the Greek-sounding word and parses it through Hebrew morphology as a 'stone tablet of revelation,' or (b) the original Hebrew 'even gilyon' was heard by Greek speakers as 'euangelion.' Either way, this is a uniquely Hebrew phenomenon — a back-translator from Greek would simply transliterate εὐαγγέλιον, not construct a Hebrew compound.

Uses עַמִּים וּלְאוּמִּים ('peoples and nations', H5971+H3816) — a standard OT poetic word pair (Gen 25:23, Ps 2:1, Isa 34:1, 51:4). Greek has the four-fold πᾶν ἔθνος καὶ φυλὴν καὶ γλῶσσαν καὶ λαόν ('every nation and tribe and tongue and people'). A back-translator from Greek would reproduce four terms, not the classic Hebrew two-term parallelism.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'hovering' (רחף — Genesis creation verb). Greek: 'flying' (πετόμενον). Different verbs with vastly different theological weight.
Hebrew: 'even gilyon' (a Hebrew compound — stone tablet / proclamation-tablet). Greek: εὐαγγέλιον αἰώνιον ('eternal gospel'). Greek adds 'eternal' (αἰώνιον) which is absent from Hebrew.
Hebrew: 'peoples and nations' (two categories). Greek: 'every nation, tribe, tongue, and people' (four categories).
translation_notes: 'Hovering' for rochef preserves the Genesis 1:2 creation connection — the same Spirit-hovering verb.
'Proclamation-tablet' for even gilyon: the second element (gilyon) means 'tablet/scroll of revelation' (cf. Isa 8:1). The compound suggests a written decree being carried through the heavens.
הַדָּרִים (ha-darim — 'those dwelling') uses a post-biblical Hebrew participial form from דור, rather than the standard biblical הַיֹּשְׁבִים from ישב (H3427).
textual_notes: Genesis 1:2 — וְרוּחַ אֱלֹהִים מְרַחֶפֶת עַל פְּנֵי הַמָּיִם ('and the Spirit of God was hovering over the face of the waters'). The same rare verb now describes a messenger hovering in mid-heaven with a proclamation.

verses.translation: And he said{H559} with a great{H1419} voice{H6963}: Fear{H3372} YHWH{H3068} and make{H6213} your prayer{H8605} to him, for the day{H3117} of judgment{H1779} has come{H935}; and make{H6213} prayer{H8605} to the one who created{H1254} the heavens{H8064} and the earth{H776} and the sea{H3220} and the wells{H875}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses הַבְּאֵרוֹת (ha-be'erot — 'the wells', H875). Greek says πηγὰς ὑδάτων ('springs/fountains of waters'). A back-translator from Greek would use מַעְיְנוֹת מַיִם ('springs of water'), not בְּאֵרוֹת ('wells'). Be'erot are DUG wells — the patriarchal wells of Abraham and Isaac (Gen 21:25-30, 26:15-22), covenant landmarks that were the subject of disputes and oaths (Beer-sheva = 'well of the oath'). The Hebrew creation list — heavens, earth, sea, wells — includes human-accessed subterranean water as part of the created order. This is a uniquely Hebraic perspective.

Uses תְּפִילָּה (tefillah — 'prayer', H8605) TWICE where Greek uses δότε αὐτῷ δόξαν ('give him glory') and προσκυνήσατε ('worship/bow down'). These are entirely different actions: prayer vs. glory-giving, prayer vs. prostration. A back-translator from Greek would use הָבוּ לוֹ כָּבוֹד ('give him glory') and הִשְׁתַּחֲווּ ('bow down'), not the tefillah idiom.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'wells' (בארות — dug wells). Greek: 'springs of waters' (πηγὰς ὑδάτων). Different water source — patriarchal wells vs. natural springs.

Hebrew: 'the day of judgment' (היום הדין). Greek: 'the hour of his judgment' (ἡ ὥρα τῆς κρίσεως αὐτοῦ). Hebrew uses 'day' (broader); Greek uses 'hour' (more specific). Greek adds 'his' which Hebrew lacks.
Hebrew: 'make prayer to him' (twice). Greek: 'give him glory' + 'worship him who made.' Different concepts — prayer vs. giving glory and bowing down.
translation_notes: 'Wells' for be'erot — these are dug wells, distinct from springs (ma'ayanot) or fountains (maqorot). The patriarchal association is inescapable.
'Prayer' for tefillah — this word encompasses petition, intercession, and communion with God. It is the standard word for Jewish liturgical prayer.
textual_notes: The creation list (heavens, earth, sea, wells) echoes Exodus 20:11 — 'For in six days YHWH made the heavens and the earth, the sea and all that is in them.' But the Hebrew substitutes 'wells' for 'all that is in them,' grounding the cosmic creation in the tangible, patriarchal landscape.

verses.translation: And after this voice{H6963} came{H935} another{H312} messenger{H4397} and cried out{H6817}: Fallen{H5307}, fallen{H5307} is Bavel{H894}, the great{H1419} city{H5892}, for she silenced{H8252} all{H3605} the peoples{H5971} with the wine{H3196} of her harlotry{H2184}.

one_way_hebrew: DIRECT QUOTE from Isaiah 21:9: נָפְלָה נָפְלָה בָּבֶל — 'Fallen, fallen is Babylon.' The Hebrew preserves Isaiah's exact wording with the doubled verb for emphasis.

CRITICAL — CONSONANTAL TEXT: The consonants ה-ש-ק-י-ט can ONLY derive from the root ש-ק-ט (shaqqat — 'to be quiet/still', H8252). The hifil הִשְׁקִיט means 'she silenced/quieted.' Greek says πεπότικεν ('she has made to drink', from ποτίζω). If the root were שקה (to give drink, H8248), the hifil 3fs would end in ת-ה (tav-he): הִשְׁקְתָה — but the consonantal text ends in ט (tet), proving the root is שקט. The Hebrew says Bavel SILENCED the nations with her wine; the Greek says she made them DRINK. A back-translator from Greek 'made drink' would use הִשְׁקְתָה (from שקה), which has completely different consonants. This is among the strongest consonantal one-way markers in the chapter.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'she silenced' (השקיט from שקט — 'to silence/quiet'). Greek: 'she made to drink' (πεπότικεν from ποτίζω). Entirely different verbs. The Hebrew image is drugging nations into passivity/silence; the Greek image is forcing them to drink.
Greek adds θυμός ('wrath/passion'): 'the wine of the wrath (θυμοῦ) of her fornication.' Hebrew has only 'the wine of her harlotry' — no wrath.
translation_notes: 'Silenced' for hishqit (hifil of שקט) — Bavel drugged the nations into stupor and silence with the wine of her harlotry. This is a more sinister image than merely 'making them drink' — she rendered them mute and passive.
Uses בָּבֶל (Bavel, H894) — the Hebrew name for Babylon, used throughout the OT from Genesis 11:9 onward.
textual_notes: Isaiah 21:9 — 'Fallen, fallen is Babylon (נָפְלָה נָפְלָה בָּבֶל), and all the graven images (פסילי) of her gods are shattered to the ground.' The Hebrew Revelation preserves the Isaiah source text; the Greek paraphrases it.

The wordplay potential: השקיט (silence) sounds close to השקה (give drink). The Hebrew author may have deliberately chosen the 'silence' verb knowing its phonetic proximity to 'drink,' achieving a double meaning — she both drugged them (drink) and silenced them.

verses.translation: And after this came{H935} the third{H7992} messenger{H4397} and said{H559} with a great{H1419} voice{H6963}: If{H518} any one{H259} shall make{H6213} his prayer{H8605} to the graven-image{H6459} and the beast{H2416} and receive{H3947} the mark upon his hand{H3027} or upon his forehead{H4696} —

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses פֶּסֶל (pesel, H6459 — 'graven image') — the exact word from the Second Commandment: לֹא תַעֲשֶׂה לְךָ פֶסֶל (Ex 20:4 — 'You shall not make for yourself a graven image'). Greek uses εἰκών ('image'). A back-translator from Greek εἰκών would use צֶלֶם (tselem — 'image') or דְּמוּת (demut — 'likeness'), NOT the Ten Commandments word pesel. The Hebrew author explicitly frames beast-worship as a violation of the Second Commandment.

Uses חַיָּה (chayyah — 'living-creature', H2416) for the 'beast' — the SAME word used for the living-creatures around the throne in verse 3 (הָאַרְבַּע חַיּוֹת). The beast is ironically called a 'living thing.' Greek uses θηρίον ('wild beast') — a specifically negative term. A back-translator from Greek θηρίον would use a pejorative term, not the neutral chayyah.

Continues using תְּפִילָּה (tefillah — 'prayer') where Greek has προσκυνεῖ ('worships/bows down'). The Hebrew consistently frames false worship as 'prayer' — the same word used for legitimate prayer to YHWH.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'graven-image' (פסל — Second Commandment term). Greek: 'image' (εἰκών — neutral term for any image). Different theological framing.
Hebrew: 'beast' (חיה — neutral 'living-creature'). Greek: 'wild beast' (θηρίον). Different connotation — the Hebrew's ironic use of chayyah is lost in Greek.
Hebrew: 'make his prayer to' (תפילתו). Greek: 'worships' (προσκυνεῖ). Prayer vs. prostration.
translation_notes: 'Graven-image' for pesel — this is the specific carved/hewn idol, as opposed to מַסֵּכָה (massechah — 'molten image'). The distinction matters: a pesel is hand-made.
סִימָן (siman — 'sign/mark') is a post-biblical Hebrew term common in rabbinic literature (b. Shabbat 55a, etc.). It has no standard Strong's number.
textual_notes: Exodus 20:4-5 — לֹא תַעֲשֶׂה לְךָ פֶסֶל... לֹא תִשְׁתַּחֲוֶה לָהֶם ('You shall not make a graven image... you shall not bow down to them'). The Hebrew Revelation recasts the beast-worship warning using the exact Torah prohibition language.

verses.translation: this one shall drink{H8354} from the wine{H3196} of the wrath{H2740} of YHWH{H3068} which is in the cup{H3563} of fury{H2740}, and shall be punished{H6064} with fire{H784} and sulfur{H1614} before{H6440} his holy{H6918} messengers{H4397} and the lamb{H7716}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses חֲרוֹן (charon, H2740 — 'fierce/burning anger') TWICE — once for the wine and once for the cup. This is the specific OT word for YHWH's burning anger (Ex 32:12; Num 25:4, 32:14; Josh 7:26; 2 Kings 23:26; Isa 13:9,13). Greek uses θυμός ('passion/wrath') for both. Charon specifically denotes HOT anger — a burning rage. A back-translator from the more generic Greek θυμός would not independently select charon both times.

Uses כּוֹס (kos, H3563 — 'cup') — the prophetic judgment cup (Isa 51:17,22; Jer 25:15-28; Ps 75:8: 'In YHWH's hand there is a cup, and the wine is foaming'). Greek ποτήριον ('drinking vessel') is generic. The Hebrew carries the full weight of the prophetic judgment-cup tradition.

Uses וְיֵעָנֵשׁ (ye'anesh — 'shall be punished', from ענש H6064). Greek says βασανισθήσεται ('shall be tormented'). The Hebrew verb means judicial punishment — a fine or penalty. The Greek means torture/torment. A back-translator from 'tormented' would use יְעֻנֶּה (ye'unneh — from ענה, to afflict/torture), not the judicial ענש.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'punished' (ענש — legal penalty). Greek: 'tormented' (βασανίζω — tortured). Different penal concept — judicial sentence vs. active torture.
Hebrew: 'wrath of YHWH' (חרון יהוה). Greek: 'wrath of God' (θυμοῦ τοῦ θεοῦ). Tetragrammaton vs. generic divine title.
translation_notes: 'Wrath' and 'fury' for the two occurrences of charon — the doubled use intensifies YHWH's burning anger. The cup is ITSELF fury, filled with the wine of fury.
'Punished' for ye'anesh is critical — this is a legal penalty, not arbitrary torment. The punishment is judicially determined.
textual_notes: Jeremiah 25:15 — כִּי כֹה אָמַר יְהוָה... קַח אֶת כּוֹס הַיַּיִן הַחֵמָה הַזֹּאת ('For thus says YHWH... Take this cup of the wine of fury'). The Hebrew Revelation draws on the Jeremiah judgment-cup tradition.
Isaiah 51:17 — 'Rouse yourself, rouse yourself! Stand up, O Jerusalem, you who have drunk from YHWH's hand the cup (כּוֹס) of his fury (חֲמָתוֹ).' The same cup imagery.

verses.translation: And the smoke{H6227} of their punishment shall go{H1980} upward{H4605} from age{H5769} to{H5704} age{H5769}, and they shall not have rest{H4496} day{H3117} or night{H3915} — those who received{H3947} the mark and who pray{H6419} to the graven-image{H6459}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses מְנוּחָה (menuchah, H4496 — 'rest') — the specific word for the eschatological promised rest (Deut 12:9; Ruth 1:9; Ps 23:2, 95:11, 132:14). Those who worship the pesel are denied the menuchah — the sabbath rest that YHWH promised Israel. Greek ἀνάπαυσιν is a generic 'rest/cessation.' A back-translator might use menuchah, but the theological weight of the term — its connection to the promised land, the Sabbath, and eschatological rest — would be coincidental.

Uses מֵעוֹלָם וְעַד עוֹלָם (me-olam ve-ad olam — 'from age to age') — a standard OT doxological formula (Ps 41:14, 90:2, 103:17, 106:48; 1 Chr 16:36). Greek uses εἰς αἰῶνας αἰώνων ('unto ages of ages'). Both are idiomatic in their respective languages.

Continues using פֶּסֶל (pesel — 'graven image') and מִתְפַּלְּלִים (mitpallelim — 'praying') where Greek uses εἰκών ('image') and προσκυνεῖ ('worships'). The Hebrew consistently frames the sin as prayer-to-an-idol, using the Second Commandment vocabulary.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'the smoke of their punishment' (עונש — legal punishment). Greek: 'the smoke of their torment' (βασανισμός — torment). Same distinction as v10.
Hebrew: 'who pray to the graven-image' (מתפללים לפסל). Greek: 'who worship the beast and his image and receive the mark of his name' (expanded list). Hebrew is more concise.
translation_notes: עוֹנֶשׁ (onesh — 'punishment') is from the root ענש (H6064). It denotes a legally imposed penalty — the same root used in v10.
'From age to age' for me-olam ve-ad olam — this captures the Hebrew temporal concept better than 'forever and ever.' The Hebrew עוֹלָם means a long but bounded age/era.
textual_notes: Isaiah 34:10 — 'Night and day it shall not be quenched; its smoke shall go up from age to age (מֵעוֹלָם וְעַד עוֹלָם — me-olam ve-ad olam).' The Hebrew Revelation quotes Isaiah 34's judgment oracle against Edom verbatim.

verses.translation: Herein is the hope{H8615} of the holy-ones{H6918}, and herein are those who do{H6213} the commandments{H4687} of YHWH{H3068} and believe{H539} in Yeshua{H3442}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses תִּקְוָה (tiqvah, H8615 — 'hope'). Greek uses ὑπομονή ('patience/endurance'). A back-translator from Greek 'patience' would write סַבְלָנוּת (savlanut — 'patience') or קַוָּאי (qavvai — 'enduring'), NOT tiqvah ('hope'). These are fundamentally different concepts — hope (confident expectation of future good) vs. patience (endurance under present trial). The Hebrew says the saints have HOPE; the Greek says they have PATIENCE.

Uses the name יֵשׁוּעַ (Yeshua, H3442) — the Hebrew name meaning 'he saves' or 'salvation,' the same name as Joshua son of Nun (Neh 8:17). Greek has Ἰησοῦ (Iesou). The Hebrew form is natural; a back-translator from Greek would typically transliterate.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'hope' (תקוה). Greek: 'patience' (ὑπομονή). Entirely different concepts.
Hebrew: 'commandments of YHWH' (מצוות יהוה). Greek: 'commandments of God' (τὰς ἐντολὰς τοῦ θεοῦ). Tetragrammaton vs. θεός.
Hebrew: 'believe in Yeshua' (מאמינים בישוע). Greek: 'the faith of Jesus' (τὴν πίστιν Ἰησοῦ). Hebrew has active believing; Greek has 'the faith of' — different grammatical construction.
translation_notes: בְּכָאן (b'chan — 'herein') is a post-biblical Hebrew demonstrative adverb, characteristic of later Hebrew linguistic registers.
'Hope' for tiqvah — the word that gives its name to the Israeli national anthem (Hatikvah). The root קוה means 'to wait/expect with confidence.'
textual_notes: Jeremiah 17:13 — מִקְוֵה יִשְׂרָאֵל יְהוָה ('The hope of Israel is YHWH'). The tiqvah of the saints is grounded in the same root as Israel's hope in YHWH.

verses.translation: And I heard{H8085} a heavenly voice from the heavens{H8064} saying{H559} to me: Write{H3789} — holy{H6918} are those who die{H4191} for the sanctification of YHWH{H3068} from now on; and it is truth{H571} that the spirit{H7307} says{H559} that they find repose{H7931} from their labors{H4639}, for their deeds{H4639} follow{H1980} after{H310} them.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses בַּת קוֹל (bat qol — literally 'daughter of a voice') — the specific RABBINIC technical term for a heavenly/divine voice (b. Berakhot 3a; b. Sotah 48b; b. Sanhedrin 11a; m. Avot 6:2). This is THE standard rabbinic term for post-prophetic divine communication. Greek simply says φωνήν ('a voice'). NO back-translator from Greek would introduce the specifically rabbinic bat qol terminology. This is among the strongest proofs of Hebrew authorship in the entire chapter — it embeds the text within the rabbinic linguistic world.

CRITICAL: Uses קִידּוּשׁ יַהְוֶה (qiddush YHWH — 'sanctification of YHWH') — the concept of קִידּוּשׁ הַשֵּׁם (qiddush ha-shem — 'sanctification of the Name'), which in rabbinic tradition means MARTYRDOM — dying to sanctify God's name (b. Sanhedrin 74a-b; Sifra Emor 9:5). Greek says ἐν κυρίῳ ἀποθνῄσκοντες ('dying in the Lord'). 'Dying IN the Lord' (Greek) means dying while belonging to the Lord. 'Dying FOR the sanctification of YHWH' (Hebrew) means dying as an act of martyrdom to sanctify the divine Name. These are ENTIRELY different theological concepts. No back-translator would introduce the qiddush ha-shem concept from the Greek.

Uses שׁוֹכְנִים (shochenim — 'dwelling/finding repose', from שכן H7931) — the root of שְׁכִינָה (Shekinah, God's dwelling presence). Greek uses ἀναπαύσονται ('they shall rest'). A back-translator from Greek would use יָנוּחוּ (yanuchu — 'they shall rest', from נוח H5117), not the theologically loaded שכן. The Hebrew says the martyrs dwell in God's own Shekinah-presence — their rest is a dwelling with God.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: bat qol ('heavenly voice' — rabbinic technical term). Greek: φωνήν ('a voice'). The Hebrew carries a whole theology of divine communication absent from Greek.
Hebrew: 'those who die for the sanctification of YHWH' (martyrdom concept). Greek: 'the dead who die in the Lord' (belonging to the Lord). Different theology of death.
Hebrew: 'they find repose' (שוכנים — Shekinah-dwelling verb). Greek: 'they shall rest' (ἀναπαύσονται — generic rest). Different quality of afterlife experience.
translation_notes: 'Heavenly voice' for bat qol — this translates the rabbinic concept rather than the literal 'daughter of a voice.' The bat qol is how God communicates after the cessation of prophecy.
'Sanctification' for qiddush — preserving the Hebrew martyrdom concept. In rabbinic tradition, dying al qiddush ha-shem ('for the sanctification of the Name') is the highest form of witness.
מֵעַכְשָׁיו (me-achshav — 'from now') is a characteristically post-biblical Hebrew temporal adverb; the biblical equivalent would be מֵעַתָּה (me-attah, H6258).
textual_notes: The bat qol concept appears throughout rabbinic literature as the mode of divine communication after the last prophets. Its presence here places the text within a Hebrew-speaking Jewish milieu that is aware of post-biblical theological developments.

Leviticus 22:32 — וְלֹא תְחַלְּלוּ אֶת שֵׁם קָדְשִׁי וְנִקְדַּשְׁתִּי בְּתוֹךְ בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל ('You shall not profane my holy name, and I will be sanctified among the children of Israel'). This is the Torah root of the qiddush ha-shem concept.

verses.translation: And I saw{H7200} one{H259} white{H3836} cloud{H6051}, and upon it sat{H3427} one like the likeness{H1823} of a man{H120}, and upon his head{H7218} a crown{H3804} of gold{H2091}, and in his hand{H3027} one{H259} sickle{H2770}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses כִּדְמוּת (ki-demut — 'like the likeness of', H1823) — the word דְּמוּת is from Genesis 1:26: 'Let us make man in our image, according to our likeness (דְּמוּתֵנוּ).' Greek has ὅμοιον υἱῷ ἀνθρώπου ('like a son of man') — a Daniel 7:13 reference. The Hebrew author uses the Genesis creation word (demut) rather than the Aramaic bar enash (son of man) idiom. A back-translator from Greek would write כְּבַר אֱנָשׁ ('like a son of man'), the Daniel phrase, not the Genesis demut.

Uses כֶּתֶר (keter, H3804 — 'crown') — the royal/imperial crown of Persian origin (Esth 1:11, 2:17, 6:8). Greek uses στέφανον ('wreath/crown'). The Hebrew keter is the sovereign's diadem; the Greek stephanos is a victor's wreath. A back-translator from Greek stephanos would use עֲטָרָה (atarah — 'wreath-crown'), not keter.

Uses חֶרְמֵשׁ (chermesh, H2770 — 'sickle') — the Israelite harvest sickle (Deut 16:9: 'From when the sickle (חֶרְמֵשׁ) is first put to the standing grain'; Deut 23:26). Greek uses δρέπανον ('sickle'). Both mean sickle, but the Hebrew carries the specific Deuteronomic agricultural-legal association.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'like the likeness of a man' (ki-demut adam — Genesis creation language). Greek: 'like a son of man' (ὅμοιον υἱῷ ἀνθρώπου — Daniel 7:13 language). Different OT allusion.
Hebrew: 'crown' (keter — sovereign's diadem). Greek: 'crown' (stephanos — victor's wreath). Different type of crown.
translation_notes: 'Likeness' for demut — preserving the Genesis 1:26 creation connection. The cloud-figure is described using the vocabulary of human creation.
'Crown' for keter — the Persian royal crown, not a laurel wreath. This is the crown of absolute sovereignty.
textual_notes: Daniel 7:13 (Aramaic) — כְּבַר אֱנָשׁ ('like a son of man'). The Hebrew Revelation's choice of דמות over the Danielic phrase suggests the author thinks in Hebrew categories (Genesis) rather than Aramaic ones (Daniel), even when describing the same vision.
Ezekiel 1:26 — כְּמַרְאֵה אָדָם ('like the appearance of a man'). Ezekiel's throne vision uses a similar construction — 'like' + a word for appearance + 'man.'

verses.translation: And another{H312} messenger{H4397} went out{H1980} from the house{H1004} of prayer{H8605} and cried out{H6817} with a great{H1419} voice{H6963} to the one sitting{H3427} upon the cloud{H6051}: Strike{H5221} with your sickle{H2770} and reap{H7114}, for the time{H6256} of the harvest{H7105} has come{H935}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses מִבֵּית הַתְּפִילָּה (mi-beit ha-tefillah — 'from the house of prayer', H1004+H8605). Greek says ἐκ τοῦ ναοῦ ('from the temple'). The Hebrew uses 'house of prayer' — the phrase from Isaiah 56:7 (כִּי בֵיתִי בֵּית תְּפִלָּה יִקָּרֵא לְכָל הָעַמִּים — 'for my house shall be called a house of prayer for all peoples'). A back-translator from Greek ναός ('temple') would use הֵיכָל (heichal) or בֵּית הַמִּקְדָּשׁ (beit hamikdash), not the Isaiah-specific 'house of prayer.' Same distinction as Revelation 21:22.

Uses הַךְ (hach — 'strike/smite', imperative of נכה H5221). Greek uses πέμψον ('send/thrust'). The Hebrew is viscerally violent — STRIKE with your sickle. The Greek is mechanical — 'send your sickle.' A back-translator from Greek would use שְׁלַח (shelach — 'send'), not the warrior-verb nakah.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'from the house of prayer' (בית התפילה). Greek: 'from the temple' (ναός). Different designation for the sacred space.
Hebrew: 'strike with your sickle' (הך — smiting verb). Greek: 'send your sickle' (πέμψον — sending verb). Different action.
Hebrew: 'the time of the harvest' (העת הקצירה). Greek: 'the hour to reap has come' (ἦλθεν ἡ ὥρα θερίσαι). Hebrew uses 'time/season' (עת); Greek uses 'hour' (ὥρα).
translation_notes: 'Strike' for hach preserves the martial force of the Hebrew — the harvest is depicted as a battle.
'House of prayer' echoes Isaiah 56:7, which Yeshua quotes in Matthew 21:13 / Mark 11:17. The Hebrew consistently uses this designation instead of 'temple.'
textual_notes: Joel 4:13 (Hebrew; 3:13 English) — שִׁלְחוּ מַגָּל כִּי בָשַׁל קָצִיר ('Put in the sickle, for the harvest is ripe'). This is the primary OT source for the harvest-judgment imagery in verses 14-19.

verses.translation: And the one sitting{H3427} upon the cloud{H6051} struck{H5221} with his sickle{H2770} and reaped{H7114}.

one_way_hebrew: Continues הִכָּה (hikkah — 'struck', from נכה H5221) where Greek has ἔβαλεν ('cast/threw'). The Hebrew image is of striking/smiting with the sickle, like a warrior in battle; the Greek is of casting the sickle.
greek_deviations: Hebrew is notably more concise — just 'he struck with his sickle and reaped.' Greek adds ἐπὶ τὴν γῆν ('upon the earth') and ἐθερίσθη ἡ γῆ ('and the earth was reaped'). The Hebrew is characteristically terse.

verses.translation: And another{H312} messenger{H4397} went{H1980} to the heavens{H8064}, and in his hand{H3027} was one{H259} sickle.

one_way_hebrew: Uses a DIFFERENT word for sickle: מַעְגָּל (ma'agal — consonants מ-ע-ג-ל), distinct from both חֶרְמֵשׁ (chermesh, vv. 14-16) and מַגָּל (maggal, v. 18). The form ma'agal relates to עגל ('round/circular') — suggesting a curved blade for grape-cutting, distinguished from the straight grain-sickle (chermesh). The Hebrew author uses THREE distinct cutting tools; Greek uses the same word δρέπανον for all. A back-translator from Greek, seeing the same word throughout, would use one Hebrew word consistently.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'went TO the heavens' (הלך לשמים — ascending direction). Greek: 'came OUT OF the temple which is in heaven' (ἐξῆλθεν ἐκ τοῦ ναοῦ τοῦ ἐν οὐρανῷ — exiting direction). Different spatial perspectives.
Greek adds ὀξύ ('sharp') to describe the sickle — absent from Hebrew here (the 'sharpness' appears later in v. 18 via the altar-messenger's command).
translation_notes: מַעְגָּל (ma'agal) — from the root עגל ('round'). Possibly a curved vintner's blade, distinct from the grain-harvest chermesh. The consonantal distinction (מ-ע-ג-ל vs. מ-ג-ל) is deliberate.

verses.translation: And another{H312} messenger{H4397} came out{H3318} from the altar{H4196}, and he had authority{H4474} over the fire{H784}, and he cried out{H6817} with a great{H1419} voice{H6963} to the one who had the sickle{H4038} and said{H559}: Strike{H5221} with your sickle{H4038} and harvest{H7114} the grapes{H6025} of the land{H776}, for its fruits{H6529} are [ripened{H1310}]. [19] And the messenger{H4397} struck{H5221} with his sickle{H4038} and harvested{H7114} the grapes{H6025} of the land{H776} and cast{H2236} them into the great{H1419} winepress{H3342} of the wrath{H2740} of YHWH{H3068}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses מַגָּל (maggal, H4038 — 'sickle') — the SAME word from Joel 4:13 (Hebrew; 3:13 English): שִׁלְחוּ מַגָּל כִּי בָשַׁל קָצִיר ('Put in the sickle, for the harvest is ripe'). The Hebrew Revelation directly echoes Joel's grape-harvest judgment using Joel's exact vocabulary. Greek uses δρέπανον throughout.

CRITICAL: Uses וְזָרַק (ve-zaraq — 'and he cast/threw', H2236) — the specific PRIESTLY verb for throwing/sprinkling sacrificial blood against the altar (Ex 24:6,8; 29:16,20; Lev 1:5,11; 3:2,8,13; 7:2,14; 17:6; Num 18:17; 2 Kings 16:13,15; Ezek 43:18). The grapes are THROWN into the winepress as sacrificial blood is thrown against the altar. Greek uses ἔβαλεν ('cast/threw' — generic). A back-translator from Greek would use הִשְׁלִיךְ (hishlich — 'threw', H7993), the common word for throwing. No translator would choose the priestly sacrificial zaraq unless thinking in priestly-sacrificial categories.

Uses יֶקֶב (yeqev, H3342 — 'winepress') — the lower collection vat where grape juice flows (Num 18:27; Deut 15:14; Isa 5:2; Joel 2:24, 4:13). Greek uses ληνός ('winepress'). Both mean winepress, but the Hebrew yeqev is technically the lower basin, distinct from the upper treading platform (גַּת, gat).

Uses מֶמְשָׁלָה (memshalah, H4474 — 'authority/dominion') for the angel's power over fire. This is the creation-dominion word from Genesis 1:16 (the luminaries given memshalah over day and night). Greek ἐξουσίαν ('authority') is generic.
greek_deviations: Hebrew combines Greek verses 18-19 into a single verse (the [19] marker shows where the Greek verse break falls).
Hebrew: 'its fruits are ripened' (נתבשל — from בשל, 'cooked/ripened'). Greek: 'her grapes are fully ripe' (ἤκμασαν). The Hebrew uses a cooking metaphor for ripeness.

Hebrew: 'he cast (zaraq — priestly verb) into the great winepress of the wrath of YHWH.' Greek: 'he cast (ἔβαλεν — generic) into the great winepress of the wrath of God.' Priestly verb + Tetragrammaton vs. generic verb + θεός.
translation_notes: נִתְבַּשֵּׁל (nitbashshel — hitpael of בשל H1310 — 'cooked/ripened') in brackets [נתבשל], suggesting editorial uncertainty about the reading. The verb literally means 'cooked themselves' — a vivid metaphor for fruit ripening in the sun.
'Cast' for zaraq — this priestly blood-sprinkling verb transforms the winepress scene into a cosmic sacrifice. The grapes-as-blood are ritually thrown, not merely tossed.
The Hebrew verse combines Greek 14:18-19, reflecting a different verse division in the Hebrew tradition.
textual_notes: Joel 4:13 (Hebrew) — שִׁלְחוּ מַגָּל כִּי בָשַׁל קָצִיר בֹּאוּ רְדוּ כִּי מָלְאָה גַּת הֵשִׁיקוּ הַיְקָבִים ('Send the sickle, for the harvest is ripe. Come, tread, for the winepress is full, the vats overflow'). The Hebrew Revelation echoes Joel's vocabulary: מגל (sickle), בשל (ripe), and יקב (winepress-vat).
Isaiah 63:3 — 'I have trodden the winepress (פּוּרָה) alone... their lifeblood was sprinkled (וְיֵז) on my garments.' The cosmic winepress of divine judgment has deep prophetic roots.

verses.translation: And the winepress{H3342} was outside{H2351} the city{H5892}, and the blood{H1818} from the winepress{H3342} went{H1980} up to the bridle{H7448} of the horses{H5483}, for a distance{H1870} of a thousand{H505} and six{H8337} hundred{H3967} field-plots{H7704}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses קִבְרוֹת הַשָּׂדֶה (qivrot ha-sadeh — 'field-plots') as the unit of measurement — the SAME uniquely Hebrew measurement that appears in Revelation 21:16 (12,000 field-plots). Greek uses σταδίων ('stadia' — a Greek athletic measurement unit). A back-translator from Greek would transliterate as סְטַדְיוֹן or use a standard Hebrew measure like אַמָּה (ammah — 'cubit') or מִיל (mil — 'mile'). No translator from Greek would independently construct a Hebrew land-measurement idiom. The consistent use of qivrot ha-sadeh across BOTH chapters (14 and 21) confirms it is a genuine Hebrew measurement system, not a one-time anomaly.

Uses רֶסֶן (resen, H7448 — 'bridle/halter') — used in Isaiah 30:28 and Psalm 32:9. Greek χαλινός also means 'bridle,' but the Hebrew word carries the prophetic association from Isaiah 30:28 where YHWH puts a resen on the nations to lead them astray.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'a thousand and six hundred field-plots' (קברות השדה). Greek: 'a thousand and six hundred stadia' (σταδίων). The numbers match but the measurement units are entirely different — a uniquely Hebrew agrarian unit vs. a Greek athletic unit.
translation_notes: קִבְרוֹת (qivrot) — possibly related to קֶבֶר (qever — 'grave/burial-plot') used as a standardized land-area unit, comparable to how 'acre' originally meant 'the amount of land one yoke of oxen could plow in a day.' The meaning is 'measured field sections.' Compare Kibroth-hattaavah (Num 11:34).
'Field-plots' preserves the agricultural/land-measurement sense without imposing the Greek athletic 'stadia.'
textual_notes: This verse maps to Greek 14:20. The Hebrew chapter has 19 verses where the Greek has 20, because Hebrew verse 18 combines Greek verses 18-19.
The measurement '1,600 field-plots' — the number 1,600 = 4 × 4 × 100, potentially symbolic of completeness (4 = earth's compass points, 100 = fullness).

chapter_notes.source_note: Chapter 13 appears to be missing from the Ele Ha-Sodot source. This chapter's verse 19 maps to Greek 14:20. The Hebrew text has 19 verses where the Greek has 20 (Hebrew v18 combines Greek vv. 18-19).
chapter_notes.summary: Revelation 14 in Hebrew contains an extraordinary density of one-way translation markers — linguistic features that can only originate in Hebrew and could not arise from back-translation of the Greek. The chapter draws on a remarkably wide range of Hebrew sources: Genesis creation language (רחף/hovering v6, דמות/likeness v14), Exodus/Sinai vocabulary (קולות/thunders v2, פסל/graven-image vv9,11, חרמש/sickle v14), Levitical priestly terminology (זרק/cast-as-sacrifice v18, קברות השדה/field-plots v19), Psalm language (מזמרים/singing v3, רמיה/deceit v5, כנור/harp v2), and prophetic texts (Isaiah 21:9 quoted verbatim in v8, Joel 4:13 echoed in vv15-18). Most striking are: (1) The consonantal proof in v8 that השקיט derives from שקט ('silence') not שקה ('give drink') — Bavel SILENCED the nations, a reading impossible to derive from the Greek. (2) The rabbinic technical term בת קול (bat qol — 'heavenly voice', v13), which embeds the text within a post-biblical Jewish linguistic world. (3) The martyrdom concept קידוש יהוה (qiddush YHWH — 'sanctification of the Name', v13), a specifically rabbinic theological category absent from the Greek. (4) The אֵוַן גֵּילִיוֹן compound (v6), which phonetically resembles εὐαγγέλιον but parses as a Hebrew 'proclamation-tablet.' (5) The consistent use of תפילה ('prayer') where Greek has 'worship/glory' — the Hebrew author frames all divine encounter as prayer. (6) The use of קברות השדה ('field-plots') as a measurement unit in BOTH chapters 14 and 21, confirming a consistent Hebrew measurement system with no Greek equivalent. (7) The distinction between רוח ('spirit', v5) and Greek στόμα ('mouth') — the Hebrew locates integrity in the inner spirit rather than outward speech. The chapter uses the Tetragrammaton (יהוה) consistently where Greek has θεός, and the Passover-lamb term שֶׂה where Greek has the generic ἀρνίον.
